A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same retrieval framework, renamed from SVDR to SIDR. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval experiments, latency measurements, ablations, and simulations in Sections 6–7 and Appendices A–D, including Wikipedia QA and BEIR results.

after.justification: V2 retains original retrieval and efficiency results and adds term-weighting/expansion experiments and hybrid retrieval cost comparisons in Appendices D–E.

M1.justification: The core encoder, binary token representation, and combined contrastive loss remain unchanged; late parametric search corresponds to v1's beta search with reranking. V2 adds lexical-only and binarized variants, including training without document expansion, and combinations using a different second-stage retriever (Appendices D–E). V1's alpha-search procedure is no longer presented.

E1.justification: Both versions cover Wikipedia QA with NQ, TriviaQA, and WebQuestions, MS MARCO passage ranking, and zero-shot retrieval on the same 12 BEIR datasets. V1 Appendix A already contains the coverage emphasized in v2's main text. The new analyses use existing NQ/Wikipedia coverage.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 4, v2 Table 2 adds uniCOIL, SPLADE, ANCE, LexMAE, SPLADE-v2, Contriever, GTR-base, E5-base, and Dragon to the reported BEIR comparison. Appendix E adds several BM25/SIDR-beta retrieval and reranker combinations, while Appendix D introduces a BoT-overlap comparator. VDR-alpha is removed from the Wikipedia QA comparison.

E3.justification: Reported MS MARCO training changes from 20 epochs with batch size 256 (v1 Appendix A) to 40 epochs with batch size 128 (v2 Section 4.3). Latency evaluation changes from resident indexes or four index shards to accumulated searches over one-million-document batches (Appendix B). New analyses introduce matched-vocabulary controls, training-versus-inference interventions, and an embedding-count cost metric. These are documented protocol changes, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 Appendix D adds controlled ablations separating query/document term weighting from expansion and testing training–inference consistency. Appendix E adds accuracy-versus-embedding-cost analysis across retrieval/reranking combinations. The original component, negative-sampling, passage-length, and index-density analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: Both Appendix B descriptions time each operation ten times and average after excluding the maximum and minimum. Neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests; v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, ablation, training-time, and hybrid cost results. Table 1 changes NQ beta-search accuracy from 35.5/60.6/76.4 to 39.8/62.9/76.3; 39.8 top-1 already appeared in v1's ablation figure. Full-search MS MARCO and BEIR-average scores change from 34.5/44.3 to 34.2/44.7 alongside revised training settings. Reported beta-indexing time changes from 1.1 to 0.5 hours. These changes do not uniformly establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix D introduces mathematical definitions of lexical-restricted and binarized parametric representations for the new variants. The core representation and loss equations remain equivalent after notation changes. The added MLM-alignment discussion supplies conceptual rationale rather than a theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains dual-index retrieval with parameter-independent indexing and in-training retrieval. V2 broadens the headline evaluation claim from three QA benchmarks to 16 benchmarks, explicitly conditions comparisons on indexing/training costs, and highlights the existing reranking approach as a late-parametric contribution. Its abstract also specifies that non-parametric superiority over BM25 concerns in-domain datasets.

C2.justification: V2 adds an MLM-based alignment rationale, hypotheses linking out-of-domain weakness to distribution sensitivity and unavailable in-training negatives, and interpretations identifying query weighting and training–inference consistency as important mechanisms. However, it removes v1's explicit limitations concerning cross-modal retrieval and larger multilingual vocabularies.

D1.justification: V2 specifies four A100 GPUs, reports training durations, documents the new representation interventions, and changes the printed code destination from jzhoubu/VDR to jzhoubu/sidr. It omits v1's initial 50% BM25-negative schedule and Appendix C disclosures about doubling the batch for the no-negative ablation and using VDR results for the no-semi-parametric-objective condition.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reframes positioning through a retrieval taxonomy and explicit comparison with query-side semi-parametric predecessors TILDE, TILDE-v2, and SPARTA. It distinguishes its index-side contribution and contextualizes advanced baselines by training cost. V1's separate binary-representation discussion and several associated citations are removed.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around three scenarios, terminology and notation change throughout, and related work moves from Section 2 to Section 7. BEIR moves into the main evaluation, while a rationale subsection and taxonomy appendix reshape the explanation. These changes extend well beyond the SVDR-to-SIDR rename and conference-header edits.

P2.justification: Both overview figures are substantially redrawn: Figure 1 removes the scenario-selection panel, and Figure 2 adds comparisons among retriever architectures. The BEIR table is relocated and expanded, the original ablation Figure 3 becomes Table 4, and new Tables 7–8 display mechanism and cost analyses. Table grouping, captions, placement, and conference formatting also change.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency–effectiveness claim through stronger baseline comparisons, vocabulary-controlled mechanism tests, and hybrid retrieval cost analysis (Tables 2, 7–8). These address important weaknesses in v1's comparative and mechanistic evidence without adding dataset coverage. Removing useful limitations and replication details weakens transparency, and some BEIR superiority prose exceeds Table 2's results. Nevertheless, the new controls and comparisons provide a substantial overall improvement in evidential support.
